While rebuilding this site I read several guides on building a portfolio: a talk summary by a
data scientist at a games company, a careers piece from a project-management training provider, a
guide for student researchers, a blog post by a data scientist who has kept a portfolio site
going for six years, and a STEM recruiting firm's advice for science graduates. They come from very different corners, but they agree on more than I expected.

Here is what stuck with me, in my own words, and what I changed because of it.

## 1. A portfolio proves what a CV only claims

Every guide starts from the same idea. A CV says "I know R" or "I did research". A portfolio shows
the analysis, the figure and the write-up, so the reader can judge for themselves. One of the
guides sums it up neatly: show, don't tell.

**What I changed:** every project page now follows the same structure: the question, the data,
the methods, the results with figures, and what I learned. If I say I can do grouped
cross-validation, the thesis page shows the diagram and the numbers.

## 2. Lead with your best work

Reviewers are busy, and several guides point out that they may never scroll past the first screen.
So the strongest project goes first, and the order should be deliberate rather than chronological.

**What I changed:** the home page now opens with my MSc thesis as a single wide card, with the key
results on the card itself. The earlier projects follow in order of strength, not date.

## 3. Quality over quantity

Three to five well-documented projects beat fifteen thin ones. The student-research guide is blunt
about this: one project with full documentation makes a stronger impression than three poorly
presented ones.

**What I changed:** I removed pages for work I had only planned, not finished. The "learning in
public" page now says clearly what is in progress, so nothing is dressed up as more than it is.

## 4. Visual evidence

A figure from your own analysis is worth more than a stock image. The guides for data-science
portfolios all push for charts, diagrams and screenshots of real outputs.

**What I changed:** each project has at least one figure I made myself: the results chart and the
validation diagram for the thesis, a workflow diagram for the lab projects. The thumbnails on the
Projects page are those same figures, not decorations.

## 5. Be honest about your level

The data-science guides warn against listing every tool you have touched. One suggests grouping
skills by level and backing each claim with evidence from a project.

**What I changed:** the [About page](../../about.qmd) lists skills in three tiers: proficient,
working knowledge and currently developing. Nothing appears in the top tier unless I have used it
in a finished project.

## 6. Make it easy to navigate, and end with a call to action

Treat the site like a product: a clear menu, a short home page, and an obvious way to get in touch.
One guide lists "no call to action" as one of the most common mistakes.

**What I changed:** the home page is now short. The detail lives on the About, Projects and CV pages,
and every page ends with a way to contact me.

## 7. Say what did not work

The science-recruiting guide and several data-science guides both ask for a "limitations and
next steps" section. A project with honest limits reads as more credible than one that claims
everything went well.

**What I changed:** the thesis page now has a Limitations section: a test set that was not truly
independent, noisy labels, and the detail lost by plot-level features.

## 8. Keep writing

The portfolio that has lasted six years works because its owner publishes something small every
week. Long-form writing also shows communication skills that no code sample can.

**What I'm doing:** one short post a week about what I built or learned. This is the third.

---

If you are building your own portfolio, the short version is: pick your best three projects,
document each one the same way, show real figures, be honest about what you can do, and make it
easy for someone to reach you. Then keep adding to it.
